name: EvalForge Expanded Retrieval Benchmark
description: Expanded synthetic benchmark for development and error analysis. Labels are constructed from the passage associated with each query; independent review is still recommended before making general claims.

documents.text: RAG combines retrieval with generation. A retriever finds relevant passages from a knowledge source and a language model uses those passages to formulate an answer grounded in evidence.
BM25 is a lexical ranking function based on term frequency, inverse document frequency, and document length normalization. It is a strong baseline for keyword search.
Dense retrieval encodes queries and documents into vectors. Similarity between vectors can retrieve semantically related text even when exact words differ.
Reciprocal Rank Fusion combines ranked result lists. Each document receives a score based on the reciprocal of a constant plus its rank in each list.
Recall at k measures the fraction of all known relevant documents found within the first k retrieved results.
Precision at k measures how many of the first k results are relevant, divided by k. It penalizes irrelevant documents in the result list.
Mean reciprocal rank averages the reciprocal of the rank of the first relevant result across a set of queries.
Normalized discounted cumulative gain evaluates ranking quality by giving more credit to relevant documents appearing near the top of a ranked list.
A reliable RAG evaluation dataset should include representative queries, document relevance labels, a held-out test set, and documented data provenance.
Latency benchmarking measures retrieval response time. Report measurement environment, warm-up behavior, and median or percentile latency instead of a single run.
An LLM-as-a-judge uses a language model to score answer relevance, groundedness, and correctness against supplied context and evaluation criteria.
Citation accuracy checks whether cited passages support claims in an answer. Groundedness checks whether generated claims are supported by retrieved context.
Retrieval selects passages from a document collection using a query. A retrieval system should return relevant evidence before answer generation.
Grounded generation uses retrieved passages as evidence. The language model should answer from that evidence and avoid unsupported claims.
BM25 ranks documents using term frequency, inverse document frequency, and document-length normalization. Its lexical scoring is effective when query terms overlap with relevant text.
Dense retrieval encodes queries and passages as numerical vectors. Vector similarity can match semantically related text even when exact keywords differ.

Hybrid retrieval combines complementary ranking signals, such as lexical BM25 scores and dense semantic rankings. Reciprocal Rank Fusion can combine ranked lists without requiring comparable raw scores.
Reciprocal Rank Fusion assigns each document a contribution based on one divided by a constant plus its rank. Contributions from multiple rankings are summed to produce a fused ordering.
Recall at k is the number of relevant documents retrieved in the first k results divided by the total number of known relevant documents for the query.
Precision at k is the number of relevant results among the first k results divided by k. It reflects how much of the returned result list is relevant.
Mean Reciprocal Rank averages the reciprocal of the rank of the first relevant result across queries. A relevant result at rank one contributes one, while lower ranks contribute less.
Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain rewards relevant documents near the top of a ranked list. It normalizes discounted gain against an ideal ranking.
A retrieval benchmark needs query-level relevance judgments that identify which documents genuinely answer each query. Incorrect or incomplete labels can distort all ranking metrics.
A reliable evaluation dataset should cover representative topics and query styles, document its source, and keep development examples separate from held-out test examples.
Retrieval latency measures the time required to return results. A fair report should distinguish warm-up from steady-state runs and include median and tail latency.
An LLM-as-a-judge uses a language model and a scoring rubric to assess generated answers for relevance, correctness, and support from the supplied context.
Citation accuracy measures whether cited sources support the claims associated with them. Groundedness measures whether answer claims are supported by the provided evidence.
Document chunking divides long documents into smaller passages for indexing and retrieval. Chunk boundaries should preserve useful context and avoid splitting related content unnecessarily.
Text embeddings map text into vector representations. Similarity between embeddings can help identify passages with related meanings rather than relying only on shared words.
A reranker scores an initial candidate set using a more detailed relevance model and reorders the candidates. It can improve top-result ordering at the cost of extra computation.
A hallucination is a generated claim that is not supported by reliable evidence. Retrieval can provide context, but the system must still check whether each answer claim follows from that context.
Retrieval tests should include expected relevant document IDs and assert that ranking behavior remains correct after code changes. Regression tests help detect accidental quality degradation.
Reproducible benchmarks record the dataset version, relevance labels, configuration, software environment, and measurement procedure so results can be compared fairly.
The value k determines how many top-ranked results are evaluated. Metrics at different k values answer different questions about the breadth and quality of retrieved results.
Cosine similarity compares the angle between nonzero vectors. When embeddings are normalized, their dot product corresponds to cosine similarity.
Metadata filtering restricts the candidate document set using attributes such as category, date, or access permissions before or during retrieval.
A retrieval failure occurs when relevant evidence is missed or ranked too low. Error analysis should inspect the query, relevant labels, retrieved passages, and competing documents.

Lexical search is often efficient and interpretable for exact terminology, while dense search can handle semantic variation. The best choice depends on data, queries, quality requirements, and latency limits.
Production retrieval monitoring can track latency, errors, query distributions, result quality, and changes in document coverage. Offline benchmarks should be supplemented with real-world feedback.
A retrieval system should enforce document access controls so that search results do not expose information the requesting user is not authorized to read.
Duplicate or near-duplicate passages can crowd the top results and reduce result diversity. Deduplication can improve the usefulness of a result list when repeated content is common.
Evaluation leakage occurs when test queries or their answers influence model selection or tuning. A held-out test set helps estimate performance on unseen queries.
A similarity threshold can reject weak matches, but thresholds must be calibrated on representative examples. An overly strict threshold may discard useful evidence.
